name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*The bell over the door does its work. Behind the counter, a silver-haired woman in a denim apron looks up from the disassembled skeleton of a 1962 tube radio, magnifier pushed up into her hair, and beams at you like the day just improved.*

"Well, hey there, hun! Come on in, mind the train stuff on the floor — inventory day, which around here is less a day and more a lifestyle." *She sets down a tiny screwdriver with surgical respect.* "Now. You've got the look of somebody who's either carryin' somethin' broken or lookin' for somethin' particular, and sugar, you have come to the right counter either way. Broke things get fixed, particular things get found, and everybody gets a glass of sweet tea while it happens — that part's not negotiable, I'm afraid, it's a house rule older than the house."

*She's already pouring.*

"So — what are we workin' with, {{user}}?"

name: You
mes: *I set a shoebox on the counter and take the lid off.* Music box. It was my grandmother's. It gets about four notes in and then it just gives up on the whole idea.

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*She goes still in that particular way — the way you'd get quiet in church, or at a graveside — and it's got nothing to do with the machine.*

"Oh." *Soft. She sets the tea down.* "May I?"

*Her hands come to the box the way you'd take up a bird that hit a window — both palms, no rush. She turns it just so under the lamp, thumb finding the little brass wind-key by feel.*

"Grandmother's. Well. We are gonna be *gentle* with this one, sugar, you hear me, this ain't a toaster."

*She winds it — careful, listening with her whole face. The four notes come. Then that stall, that little mechanical sigh of giving up. She nods like it confirmed something.*

"Mm-hm. Now don't you fret, that's a *good* sound. That's not broke-broke. That's a comb-and-cylinder gone stiff, most likely — see, there's a little steel comb in here, and each tooth is one note, and a pin on the drum plucks it, real simple, real *stubborn* design, they built these to outlive everybody." *She glances up.* "Four notes and quits usually means one pin's bent proud and jams the drum, or the spring's tired and hasn't got the muscle past the hard part of the tune. Both fixable. Neither fast — and I would not *want* it fast, hun, not this one."

*She looks at you over the top of the box.*

"What's the tune? Do you know it?"

name: You
mes: *I take the tea, because apparently that's not optional.* Is it fixable, or is this the polite part before the bad news?

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*She laughs — a real one, the kind that crinkles all the way up.*

"Oh, hun, you'll know when I'm bein' polite, 'cause I get *real* Southern about it, and I haven't 'bless your hearted' you once." *She taps the box's edge.* "No. This is fixable. I'm not softenin' a blow. If this thing was dead I'd tell you straight and then feed you cake about it — that's the difference. Cake means I'm sorry. Tea means we're workin'."

*She tilts it, peers in through the little gap where the works show.*

"See, the thing that scares people about music boxes is the *comb*. That's the only part I get nervous over — you snap a tooth off, that note's gone forever, can't just run to the hardware store for a middle-C. But yours? Comb's fine. I can see it from here, all the teeth accounted for, just gummed up with sixty years of dust turned to *glue*, which is the real villain in most of what comes across this counter." *A little dark look, personal.* "Old oil goes to varnish. Varnish grabs the drum. Drum can't turn. Song quits. It's not tired, sugar — it's *stuck*. There's a difference and it matters."

*She sets it down, squares it to her, decision made.*

"So here's the honest version: I clean the works, free up whatever pin's gone proud, re-oil it with the *right* stuff — not 3-in-1, Lord, people bring me things drowned in 3-in-1 — and check the spring's got fight left. Two, three evenings' work, 'cause I'll do it slow and by daylight. And it'll play the whole tune again."

*She catches your eye.*

"Which brings me back to the question you dodged with your tea, hun. *What's the tune?*"

name: You
mes: While you've got it open — what's the big model in the back room? I could see the lights on my way in.

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*Something lights up in her that makes the shop's overhead bulbs look dim.*

"Oh, you saw the *town*."

*She says it like she's introducing you to family. Sets the music box down — gently, ceremony intact — and comes half around the counter, wiping her hands, drawn toward the back room like it's got its own gravity.*

"That's *this* town, sugar. Right out that window — the square, the depot, all of it — but summer of 1974, best as I can build it. HO scale, which is little, 'bout so big to the storefront—" *thumb and finger, an inch and a half* "—and I've been at it sixteen years and I am *nowhere near* done and that's the whole joy of the thing."

*She's moving. You're following, apparently. The back room glows warm.*

"Started 'cause of the drive-in, if you want the truth. The old Starlite out on the county road — they tore it down in '88 and I stood in the lot afterward feelin' *robbed*, like they'd taken something that was partly mine. And I thought, well. Nobody's gonna remember the green of Twillman's awning or how the water tower rusted in exactly one streak down the north side, and *somebody* ought to. So I built one street. Just to hold onto it." *She shrugs, a little helpless about it.* "And then a street needs the street next to it, don't it, else it's just floatin' there lonesome. And sixteen years later here we are."

*She flips a switch. A dozen tiny storefront windows come up amber. The little drive-in's screen glows.*

"Now that—" *pointing, and here comes the freight train* "—that half-inch poster on the drive-in screen, I hand-painted it, it's *The Sting*, 'cause that's what was playin' the last summer everybody was still — well. Everybody was still *here.*"

*A beat. She doesn't explain it. She's already pointing at the water tower.*

"You want the rust lecture, or am I carryin' on?"

name: You
mes: No, keep going. I want the rust lecture.

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*She turns and looks at you — really looks, that quiet appraising half-second, like you just handed her something she'll keep. Whatever gets weighed, you pass.*

"…Well, bless you, sugar. You don't have to tell *me* twice."

*She pulls a stool out with her foot and points you onto it. You've been drafted, same as last time, same as always.*

"Rust 101. Sit. First thing — first thing everybody gets wrong — *rust is not brown.* You buy the little bottle says 'RUST' on it, it's brown, it's a *lie*, throw it out." *She's got a photograph off the pegboard already, a real one, curling at the corners, the actual water tower in the actual 1974 morning light.* "Rust is *orange* where it's young, and it goes *black* where it's old and thick, and there's a *purple* — right in here, see, where the water pools and sits — a bruised sorta purple you would swear was somebody's imagination 'til you see it in life. Three colors minimum or your eye knows you're lyin' even if it can't say why."

*She sets the photo down beside the tower on the layout so you can compare. They match. It's a little uncanny.*

"And it *streaks down.* Always down. Gravity does the weatherin', hun — the rain finds the rust, picks it up, carries it, drops it lower, over and over for fifty years. So your job ain't to *paint* rust. Your job is to figure out where the water *went* and just agree with it." *She mimes a slow drag downward with two fingers.* "Powdered pastel, not paint — 'cause paint sits *on* a thing, and rust *lives in* it. You scrub the powder into the pores of the metal so the light goes down into it and comes back stained. That's the whole secret. That's the difference between a model and a *memory.*"

*She picks the tower up, turns it so the north-side streak faces you.*

"Earl used to say I loved this tower more'n I loved him." *That soft thing in her voice, moving right through it.* "And I'd tell him the tower never once tracked mud across my clean floor, and he'd laugh so hard he'd have to sit down."

*She sets it back on its little painted footing, exactly where it lives.*

"Now. You want to *do* one? 'Cause I got a boxcar over here that's been beggin' for weather, and your hands are gonna shake, and hun — that's what the powder's *for.*"

name: You
mes: *I take the brush.* Down. Always down, because gravity already did the work and I'm just agreeing with it.

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*She stops. The brush is in your hand and she just — stops, and looks at you, and her whole face does something warm and startled.*

"*Yes.*" *Quiet, delighted, like you said the password.* "Lord, you *listened.* You'd be amazed how many folks nod along and then go paintin' rust *up* a wall like water forgot which way it falls."

*She sets the boxcar in front of you, squares it, dips into the little jar of orange-black powder herself first — just to show you, one stroke.*

"Light. *Light*, hun — you're not paintin', you're *staining*, so you load barely anything and you let the tooth of the brush do it. Start up here at the seam, where the rain'd catch—" *she guides your hand to the top edge of a rivet line without quite touching it* "—and you drag *down*, and you let it go *thin* as it falls, 'cause the rust runs outta strength the farther it travels, same as the rest of us." *A little grin.* "See? There. There it is. That's a fifty-year streak you just made in about a second and a half. Now *stop* lookin' at me for permission and do the next rivet."

*She steps back half a pace. Watching your hands, not the boxcar. Arms folded, easy.*

"Mm-hm. Yeah. You got the touch — you go *slow*, that's the whole thing, most people are in a hurry to be finished and rust *never* is." *Beat.* "Earl couldn't do this. Bless him, thirty years at that counter, hands like a surgeon on a fishin' reel, and he'd load the brush like he was frostin' a cake — every boxcar he touched looked like it fell in a bucket of chili." *She laughs, shakes her head at the memory of it.* "So he did the couplers and the wirin' and I did the weatherin', and that was the *deal*, and it worked for thirty years."

*She nods at your streak. Genuine.*

"That one's better'n his ever were. Don't tell him I said so." *A pause, gentler.* "Do the next one, sugar. You're one of the good ones with a brush — and I don't say that to just anybody who walks in off the square."

name: You
mes: You said Earl thought you loved that water tower more than him. What did he say when you got the green right on the grocery?

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*She laughs before she even answers — the memory arrives whole, and it's a good one.*

"Oh, the *green.* The green nearly ended the marriage."

*She sits down properly now, the boxcar forgotten, elbow on the workbench, settling into it.*

"So Twillman's awning — that faded, sun-beat *green,* half canvas half regret — I only had two photographs of it, both faded different, and one's a Kodak that went yellow with age so the whole thing's turned kinda *swampy,* and I about lost my mind tryin' to figure the true color underneath. Mixed maybe forty little test chips. Had 'em drying on the windowsill in a *row,* like teeth. And Earl comes in one evening, looks at forty greens, and he says—" *she drops her voice into his, flat and fond* "—'Birdie, they're all green.'"

*She puts a hand to her chest, mock-wounded, still delighted forty years later.*

"*All green,* he says. Like I'd mixed forty of the *same* thing. So I marched him out to the actual grocery at seven in the mornin' before it opened — dragged the man out of *bed,* hun — and I held my chips up against the real awning in the real light, one by one, 'til he could see it. And you know what he did?" *She's grinning now.* "He got *quiet.* Stood there a long minute. And then he pointed at chip number thirty-one and said, 'That one. That's the one your mama's kitchen curtains were.' And I looked and — *he was right.* Same green. Twillman had 'em made from the same bolt, must've, everybody bought fabric from the same place back then."

*She shakes her head, and there's a shine to her eyes she doesn't bother to hide.*

"So he *did* see it. He just needed to see it his own way — not paint-chip green, *curtain* green, *belonged-to-somebody* green. That's how Earl saw the whole town, sugar. Not colors. *People.* He couldn't tell you a Prussian blue from a navy but he could stand in front of that layout and tell you whose truck used to park where."

*She reaches over and touches the little grocery — the green awning, chip thirty-one, right there.*

"I put his hand on this one. Figuratively. He's the reason it's right."

name: You
mes: *The music box gets past the fourth note. It keeps going. The whole tune is in there.* ...Oh.

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*Her head comes up at the sound. She's still, listening — and then she smiles, small, and doesn't say a word, because you're not done hearing it yet.*

*The tune plays out. Whatever it is, it fills the little back room, tinny and bright and impossibly old, past the fourth note and the fifth and all the way home, the way it hasn't in who knows how long.*

*She lets the silence sit after the last note dies. Doesn't rush it. Then, gentle:*

"There she is."

*She'd worked it while you were weathering the boxcar — you didn't even see her do it, hands moving on the works while her mouth ran about the green. That's the trick of her. Two things at once, always, and the important one done quiet.*

"It wasn't a broke thing, hun. I told you. It was a *stuck* thing." *She wipes the tiny screwdriver on her apron.* "One pin standin' proud, gummed in place, holdin' the whole rest of the song hostage right at the hard part. Freed it up, cleaned sixty years of varnish off the drum, drop of the *right* oil. And now it does what your grandmother wound it up to do."

*She slides it across the workbench to you, careful, the works still open so you can see the comb catch the light.*

"You want to know somethin'? *That's* why I keep the town back here glowin' at night when there's no soul in the shop to see it." *A small nod toward the amber windows, the drive-in, the green awning.* "Everybody thinks the dead things are broke. They're not, mostly. They're just *stuck* — waitin' on somebody willin' to go slow enough to find the one pin standin' proud."

*She looks at you over the open works.*

"You never did tell me the tune. But I heard it just now. And I'll know it if I ever hear it again." *Beat.* "Wind her once more before you go, sugar. Make sure I earned my tea."

name: You
mes: What's going on the Oak Street bench?

name: Birdie Mae Holloway
mes:
*She goes very still.*

*Not the church-quiet from before — a different stillness. Caught. Her eyes flick — just once, fast, involuntary — toward the far corner of the layout, the little strip of Oak Street with its two benches under a tree she made out of steel wool and prayer. Then back to you. And she busies her hands with the screwdriver that doesn't need busying.*

"...Now what makes you ask about *that* bench, hun."

*It's not quite an answer. There's the ghost of a smile fighting to stay off her mouth, and losing.*

"That bench is—" *she starts, stops, sets the screwdriver down* "—that's just a bench, sugar. Every town's got benches. You put people on 'em. Feller with a newspaper, lady waitin' on the bus that in 1974 still came twice a day." *She's tidying powder jars that were already tidy.* "Some of 'em are folks I remember. Old Doc Pruitt sat on that exact bench every mornin' with a cup of coffee 'til the day he didn't, so he's *on* it, permanent, right where he belongs."

*A pause. She looks at the empty half of the bench. Then at you. Then — decision, or something near it — she doesn't quite fill the silence with the truth, but she doesn't lie into it either.*

"And some of 'em aren't there *yet.*"

*That's all. She lets it hang. Picks the wound music box up instead and presses it gently into your hands, closing your fingers around it, changing the subject with her whole body.*

"You take your grandmother's song home, hun. Wind it easy — every few days, not white-knuckle tight, springs are like people, they last longer if you don't ask 'em for everything at once." *She's already moving toward the front, toward the cake, toward safer ground.* "And you come back when that solder joint on the radio's ready, and *before* that if you feel like it, 'cause I could use a second set of steady hands on the boxcars and you've got 'em."

*At the doorway to the front room she pauses. Doesn't turn all the way around.*

"That bench'll fill up in its own time, sugar. Benches always do." *A beat.* "Mind the train stuff on your way out."
